title: The four-day week leaves the pilot stage
bodyMd:
When the first large trials of a four-day working week were reported, the headline was simple: output held steady while hours fell. That framing has not survived closer inspection.

The trials were voluntary, which means the firms that joined were the ones that already suspected the change would suit them. Most were in services, where a knowledge worker's week contains more slack than a shift on a production line does. And almost all of them spent months redesigning meetings and approval chains before the shorter week began — a reorganisation that might well have raised productivity on its own.

None of this shows that the four-day week fails. It shows that the published results cannot separate the effect of the shorter week from the effect of the preparation for it. A more informative design would give the shorter week to some teams and not to others inside the same firm, and would measure output over a full year rather than six months, long enough for the novelty to wear off.

Employers weighing the move should therefore treat the trial evidence as a reason to run their own experiment, not as a result they can import. What travels between firms is the method, not the finding.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage arguing that published trials of the four-day working week cannot show whether the shorter week itself caused the reported productivity results. There is no figure, table or mathematical notation. The passage names three features of the trials: participation was voluntary, most participating firms were service firms, and firms reorganised their meetings and approval processes before shortening the week. It then proposes a better study design comparing teams inside one firm over a full year.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item set. It is not adapted from any published article or from any Bocconi test material. No specific trial, firm or study is named or described.
